title: If the digits of a multiple of nine are reversed, what happens?
description: Jia claims that reversing the digits of a multiple of nine gives another multiple of nine. The video uses the digit sum to test the claim, and then every other shuffle of the digits.
teaching_notes: One idea: a shuffle of the digits keeps the digit sum, so a multiple of nine stays a multiple of nine. Watch for students who test only one example and call it a proof, or who think the reverse is special and other shuffles are not.

video_script.why: The student knows that a number is divisible by nine when its digit sum is, and now uses the fact that a shuffle of the digits keeps the digit sum.
video_script.substitution: Compare the digit sum before and after the digits are reversed or shuffled, then test the claim on a multiple of nine.
video_script.anchor: the digits of a multiple of nine in boxes, with an arrow that reverses them
video_script.payoff_line: The claim is true for every multiple of nine

final_answer.value: (i) True for every multiple of 9 (ii) Yes, every shuffle of the digits is still a multiple of 9
final_answer.spoken: the claim is true for every multiple of nine, and every shuffle of the digits is also a multiple of nine

names.Jia: reverses the digits of a multiple of 9

hold_back: Answer: (i) True for every multiple of 9
maths_rules: a number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is divisible by 9
reversing the digits keeps the same digits, so the digit sum stays the same
a multiple of 9 has a digit sum that is a multiple of 9, so the reversed number is also a multiple of 9
any shuffle keeps the same digit sum, so it is still a multiple of 9; 648 = 9 x 72
